content: 1. GRADE 1: Annual IDA versus Annual DA for Lymphatic Filariasis Elimination The question addressed whether ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole (IDA) should be used annually instead of diethylcarbamazine and albendazole (DA) for mass drug administration (MDA) in areas where onchocerciasis is not co-endemic. The studies were conducted in lymphatic filariasis-endemic communities (caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia species) in countries using DA for elimination efforts. The quality of evidence was moderate for critical adverse events (AEs) in communities with no prior MDA, showing 50 fewer events per 100,000 people (confidence interval: 91 fewer to 52 more). For Grade 2–4 AEs, the evidence was low quality, with 11 more events per 1,000 people (confidence interval: 35 fewer to 83 more). Limitations included unclear allocation concealment, incomplete outcome data, and small sample sizes in some studies. Variations in protocols were attributed to national differences, and open-label designs introduced detection bias. 2. GRADE 2: Biannual DA versus Annual DA for Lymphatic Filariasis Elimination This question evaluated whether biannual DA is more effective than annual DA for MDA in areas where onchocerciasis is not co-endemic. The studies were conducted in lymphatic filariasis-endemic communities using DA. The quality of evidence was very low, with wide confidence intervals and small sample sizes. The outcome of interest was the reduction in prevalence at follow-up relative to baseline prevalence, accounting for variations between control and intervention groups. 3. GRADE 3: Annual IDA versus Annual IA for Lymphatic Filariasis Elimination This question compared annual IDA (ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole) with annual IA (ivermectin and albendazole) for MDA in areas where onchocerciasis is not co-endemic. For serious adverse events (SAEs) among microfilaremic individuals, the evidence was of very low quality, showing 80 fewer events per 1,000 people (confidence interval: 170 fewer to 20 more). For general AEs, the evidence was low quality, with 8 fewer events per 1,000 people (confidence interval: 163 fewer to 256 more). Limitations included unclear allocation concealment, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals. 4. GRADE 4: Biannual IA versus Annual IA for Lymphatic Filariasis Elimination This question assessed whether biannual IA is more effective than annual IA for MDA in areas co-endemic with onchocerciasis. The quality of evidence was very low, with wide confidence intervals and small sample sizes. Both studies reviewed were non-randomized trials with unclear randomization and allocation concealment. Open-label designs increased the risk of detection bias, particularly for subjective outcomes. 5. GRADE 5: Biannual Albendazole versus Annual Albendazole for Lymphatic Filariasis Elimination in Loiasis Co-Endemic Areas This question evaluated whether biannual albendazole (ALB) is more effective than annual ALB for MDA in areas co-endemic with loiasis, where ivermectin has not been distributed. The evidence was derived from a single-arm community cohort study, indirectly compared with another study. After 15 months, none of the 12 patients in the study were cleared of CFA with albendazole (600 mg). The quality of evidence was very low due to the small sample size and indirect comparisons. 6. General Observations Across Studies Many studies had limitations such as unclear allocation concealment, incomplete outcome data, and small sample sizes. Open-label designs introduced detection bias, particularly for subjective outcomes. Wide confidence intervals in several studies allowed for the possibility of clinically insignificant harms, substantial harms, or even some benefits. Variations in baseline prevalence and geographic differences were accounted for in the analysis. These findings highlight the need for more robust, randomized trials with larger sample sizes to better evaluate the efficacy and safety of different MDA regimens for lymphatic filariasis elimination.
